paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: God's people ran to Egypt and said no thanks to His rescue, and the very next thing the prophet says is "Therefore the LORD longs to be gracious to you" (Isaiah 30:18). Therefore! After all that! I would have expected a lecture, and what we get is a God who "rises to show you compassion" (Isaiah 30:18). He is also "a just God," and the same verse says, "Blessed are all who wait for Him" (Isaiah 30:18).

Waiting is hard, and the passage doesn't pretend otherwise. The Lord gives "the bread of adversity and the water of affliction," but your Teacher "will no longer hide Himself" (Isaiah 30:20). Whether you turn to the right or to the left, there's a voice behind you saying, "This is the way. Walk in it" (Isaiah 30:21). When people hear Him like that, the idols they trusted get thrown out, and the rain, the pastures and the healing come from the LORD (Isaiah 30:22-26).

The passage also says the LORD's judgment on the nations is real, and His coming is no small thing (Isaiah 30:27-33). But His people don't have to be afraid of it. They sing "as on the night of a holy festival" and walk to the mountain of the LORD, "to the Rock of Israel" (Isaiah 30:29). So when you've run off on your own again, baker, don't hide. Turn around, because He's already longing to be gracious to you.
